paper.title_en: What Becomes of the Antiferromagnetic String When Long Range Neel Order Is Lost? Exact Results
paper.abstract_en: Early string descriptions of doped antiferromagnets associate hole motion in a locally Néel-ordered background with a path-dependent antiferromagnetic string. We ask what becomes of this mechanism when long range Néel order is lost while short range antiferromagnetic correlations persist. In a singlet bond representation, the underlying basis states do not assign an oriented \(A/B\) spin registration to each bond. Therefore, any surviving long wavelength antiferromagnetic axis is naturally described as a director, \(\mathbf n\sim-\mathbf n\). Long range Néel order can nevertheless provide a global \(S^2\) lift of this director field; when that long range registration is lost, non liftable configurations of the \(RP^2\) manifold become physically accessible, opening a topologically nontrivial \(\mathbb Z_2\) sector. Its elementary defects are half vortices that globally minimize the \(RP^2\) \(σ\)-model energy within the nontrivial \(\mathbb Z_2\) sector. An \textit{a posteriori} energetic comparison further shows that the projective half vortex texture is softer than the corresponding vector reference texture. A pair of half vortices with opposite windings is logarithmically confined, \(V(R) = κ\ln\left(R/r_{\text{core}}\right)\), \(κ= πρ_s /2\). The resulting confinement is carried not by a one dimensional string but by an extended two-dimensional spin texture. Thus, the loss of long-range Néel order does not eliminate antiferromagnetic confinement but removes the global Néel lift. This activates a distinct projective mechanism in which a local path dependent string is replaced, at long wavelengths, by a global topological texture with logarithmic confinement.
